title: Mind–body dualism
description: Philosophical view that consiousness and the body are fundamentally different
wiki_lead:
In philosophy of mind, mind–body dualism denotes either that mental phenomena are non-physical, or that the mind and body are distinct and separable. Thus, it encompasses a set of views about the relationship between mind and matter, as well as between subject and object, and is contrasted with other positions, such as physicalism and enactivism, in the mind–body problem.
Aristotle shared Plato's view of multiple souls and further elaborated a hierarchical arrangement, corresponding to the distinctive functions of plants, animals, and humans: a nutritive soul of growth and metabolism that all three share; a perceptive soul of pain, pleasure, and desire that only humans and other animals share; and the faculty of reason that is unique to humans only. In this view, a soul is the hylomorphic form of a viable organism, wherein each level of the hierarchy formally supervenes upon the substance of the preceding level. For Aristotle, the first two souls, based on the body, perish when the living organism dies, whereas there remains an immortal and perpetual intellective part of mind. For Plato, however, the soul was not dependent on the physical body; he believed in metempsychosis, the migration of the soul to a new physical body. It has been considered a form of reductionism by some philosophers, since it enables the tendency to ignore very big groups of variables by its assumed association with the mind or the body, and not for its real value when it comes to explaining or predicting a studied phenomenon.
Dualism is closely associated with the thought of René Descartes (1641), who holds that the mind is a nonphysical—and therefore, non-spatial—substance. Descartes clearly identified the mind with consciousness and self-awareness and distinguished this from the physical brain as the seat of intelligence. Hence, he was the first documented Western philosopher to formulate the mind–body problem in the form in which it exists today. However, the theory of substance dualism has many advocates in contemporary philosophy such as Richard Swinburne, J. P. Moreland, E. J. Lowe, Charles Taliaferro.
Dualism is contrasted with various kinds of monism. Substance dualism is contrasted with all forms of materialism, but property dualism may be considered a form of non-reductive physicalism.

Types
Ontological dualism makes dual commitments about the nature of existence as it relates to mind and matter, and can be divided into three different types:

Substance dualism asserts that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct kinds of foundations.
Property dualism suggests that the ontological distinction lies in the differences between properties of mind and matter (as in emergentism).
Predicate dualism claims the irreducibility of mental predicates to physical predicates.


Substance or Cartesian dualism
Substance dualism asserts that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct kinds of foundations. There are different types of substance dualism. Most substance dualists hold the view that the mind and body are capable of causally affecting each other, known as interactionism. Notable defenders of substance dualism include John Foster, Stewart Goetz, Richard Swinburne and Charles Taliaferro.
Cartesian dualism, most famously defended by René Descartes, argues that there are two kinds of substances: mental and physical. Descartes states that the mental can exist outside of the body, and the body cannot think. Substance dualism is important historically for having given rise to much thought regarding the famous mind–body problem. It is compatible with theologies which claim that immortal souls occupy an independent realm of existence distinct from that of the physical world. Cartesians tend to equate the soul to the mind.

grok_lead: Mindâbody dualism is a foundational position in the philosophy of mind asserting that the mind and body are two fundamentally distinct substances, with the mind characterized as a non-physical, thinking entity and the body as a physical, extended entity. This view posits that mental states, such as thoughts and consciousness, cannot be reduced to physical processes in the brain or body, emphasizing their ontological independence. Formulated most influentially by the 17th-century French philosopher RenÃ© Descartes, dualism emerged as a response to mechanistic views of the natural world, allowing for the separation of immaterial soul-like aspects from material physiology. Descartes articulated the core arguments for dualism in his Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), particularly in the Sixth Meditation, where he contends that the mind's essence consists solely in being a thinking, non-extended thing, while the body's essence is extension without thought. He supports this distinction through the criterion of clear and distinct perception: since the mind can be conceived independently of the body (as indivisible) and vice versa (as divisible), they must be really distinct substances capable of separate existence, a possibility ensured by divine omnipotence. Despite their union in human experienceâevident in sensations like pain, which link the twoâDescartes maintains that this interaction does not undermine their metaphysical separation, though he locates the point of union in the pineal gland without fully explaining the mechanism. This framework not only aligned with Christian theology by preserving an immortal soul but also facilitated the scientific study of the body as a machine, influencing the development of modern physiology and psychology as distinct disciplines. Historically, dualism has roots in ancient philosophy, such as Plato's separation of soul and body, in which he portrayed the body as a prison for the soulâa source of deception, desires, fears, and illusions that hinder the soul's pursuit of true knowledge and moral development, as articulated in the Phaedo. Descartes' substance dualism provided a rigorous metaphysical foundation that dominated Western thought for centuries. It shaped medical practice by permitting dissection and mechanistic explanations of bodily functions without theological interference, yet it entrenched a divide that marginalized mental health in biomedicine. Proponents like John Eccles in the 20th century defended refined versions, arguing that quantum physics might allow for non-physical influences on the brain. Criticisms of dualism abound, particularly from materialist perspectives that view it as incompatible with empirical neuroscience, which demonstrates correlations between brain states and mental phenomena without requiring non-physical causation. In health contexts, the dualistic legacy has been faulted for fostering a reductive biomedical model that overlooks psychosocial factors, contributing to patient dehumanization, increased litigation, and delayed integration of holistic care as defined by the World Health Organization's emphasis on complete physical, mental, and social well-being. Philosophers critique the interaction problem: how an immaterial mind causally affects a material body remains unexplained, rendering dualism vulnerable to considerations of metaphysical economy in favor of monistic alternatives like physicalism. In contemporary discourse, dualism persists in debates within psychiatry and cognitive science, where some argue it remains empirically viable and ethically beneficial for preserving human dignity beyond neural mechanisms, while others see it as an outdated relic hindering interdisciplinary progress. Variants such as property dualismâpositing mental properties as non-physical emergents of physical substratesâattempt to address these challenges.
